content: Melasma is a condition characterized by dark discoloration of the skin, typically appearing on areas of the face that are exposed to the sun. The primary symptom of melasma is skin discoloration, which can be a significant cosmetic concern for affected individuals. The discoloration usually presents as a uniform brown color, commonly seen on the cheeks, forehead, nose, or upper lip. It is often symmetrical, meaning it appears similarly on both sides of the face. Melasma is a very common skin disorder. While it can affect anyone, young women with brownish skin tones are at the highest risk. The condition is frequently associated with the female hormones estrogen and progesterone. It is particularly common in pregnant women, women taking oral contraceptives (birth control pills), and those undergoing hormone replacement therapy (HRT) during menopause. Sun exposure is another significant risk factor, and melasma is especially prevalent in individuals living in tropical climates. A healthcare provider can typically diagnose melasma based on the appearance of the skin. In some cases, a closer examination using a Wood's lamp may be performed to guide treatment decisions. If you experience persistent darkening of the skin on your face, it is advisable to contact your healthcare provider. Treatment options for melasma include creams containing a combination of tretinoin, kojic acid, and azelaic acid, which have been shown to improve the condition. Your doctor may also recommend chemical peels or topical steroid creams. In severe cases, laser treatments may be used to remove the dark pigmentation. Avoiding sun exposure and using sunscreen are essential for both treatment and prevention of melasma. Melasma often fades over several months after stopping birth control pills, discontinuing HRT, or delivering a child. However, it may recur with subsequent pregnancies or the use of these medications. Daily use of sunscreen is not only critical for preventing melasma but also plays a vital role in reducing the risk of skin cancer and preventing wrinkles.
